decks.title: Database Concepts — Part 1: Why Databases, and the Relational Model
goals: Explain the problems of keeping data in separate files and how a DBMS solves them
Use the terms relation, tuple, attribute and domain correctly
Find the degree and cardinality of a relation, after changes, and of a Cartesian product

slides.heading: Database Concepts
slides.body_md: Part 1 — why we need **databases**, what a **DBMS** does, and the **relational model**: tuples, attributes, domains, degree and cardinality.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: problems with files, what a DBMS does, relation, tuple and attribute, domain, degree and cardinality, Cartesian product
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every school, shop and hospital keeps records. In this chapter we see why keeping them in separate files causes trouble, how a database management system fixes it, and how a relational database arranges data in tables. By the end you will count degree and cardinality without slipping.

slides.heading: Data kept in separate files
slides.body_md: Before databases, each office kept its **own file**. The same student details were typed again and again.

rows: AdmNo, name, address, phone, bus route

visual.alt: Table of three separate files of an imagined school: the admission file, the fee file and the transport file each repeat the student name, and the transport file repeats address and phone
visual.caption: The same facts typed into three files.

slides.narration: Picture an imagined school where the office, the accounts section and the transport desk each keep their own file. Look at the last column: the student name appears in all three files, and the address and phone appear twice. Every repeat is extra typing, and every repeat is a chance for a mistake.

slides.heading: Five problems of file systems

rows: New phone number in one file only
Data exists but is hard to get
Bus users with unpaid fees takes days
Anyone with the file sees everything
Fee clerk can read health notes
Programs break when the file layout changes
A new column breaks the fee program

visual.alt: Table of five file-system problems: redundancy, inconsistency, unavailability, unauthorised access and data dependence, with what goes wrong and an example from an imagined school

slides.narration: This table lists the five problems you must know. Redundancy means the same data is stored many times. Inconsistency means the copies disagree after an update. Unavailability means the data exists but is hard to get in the form you need. Unauthorised access means anyone with the file sees everything. Data dependence means programs break when the file layout changes.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the problem
slides.body_md: A phone number is changed in one file but not in another. Which problem is this?
slides.narration: Think about what has gone wrong: is data missing, or are two copies telling different stories?

slides.heading: What a DBMS does
slides.body_md: A **database** is an organised collection of related data. A **DBMS** (database management system) is the software that creates it, stores it, **checks rules** and **controls access** — for example **MySQL**.

nodes.label: DBMS (for example MySQL): stores, checks, controls access

visual.alt: Flow: users and programs send requests to the DBMS, which stores data, checks rules and controls access to the database of related tables
visual.caption: The DBMS sits between users and data

slides.narration: A database is the organised collection of related data. The database management system is the software in the middle. Users and programs never touch the data directly; they ask the system, which stores the data once, checks rules such as keys, and decides who may see what. MySQL is the system you will use in this course.

slides.heading: File system or DBMS?
columns:
**File system**

- Same data in many files
- Copies can disagree
- New report = new program
- All-or-nothing access

**DBMS**

- Data stored once, linked by keys
- One update seen everywhere
- New report = new query
- Each user sees only allowed data
slides.narration: Here is the contrast in one view. On the left, the file system repeats data, lets copies drift apart, needs a new program for every new report, and gives all-or-nothing access. On the right, a database management system stores each fact once, keeps one version, answers new questions with a query and controls who sees what.

slides.heading: A relation is a table
slides.body_md: In the **relational model**, data is kept in **relations** (tables).

slides.narration: In the relational model, data lives in tables called relations. This is the imagined student relation. Each column, such as Name, is an attribute. Each row, such as the one for Meera Iyer, is a tuple. The heading row only names the attributes; it is not a tuple, so it is never counted.

slides.heading: Tuple, attribute and domain

rows: Set of values an attribute may take

visual.alt: Table of relational terms with meanings and examples from the imagined STUDENT relation: relation, tuple, attribute, domain, degree 4 and cardinality 5

slides.narration: Learn these words as pairs. A tuple is a row, also called a record. An attribute is a column, also called a field. A domain is the set of values an attribute is allowed to take: for Class it is the list of class names in the school. Degree and cardinality are counts, which we look at next.

slides.heading: Quick check: repetition and keys
slides.body_md: True or false? A DBMS removes every repeated value, so a foreign key value may never appear in two tables.
slides.narration: Think about how two tables can be linked if no value is ever repeated.

slides.heading: Degree and cardinality
slides.body_md: **Degree** = number of **attributes** (columns). **Cardinality** = number of **tuples** (rows).

visual.alt: Table of degree and cardinality of six imagined relations, measured by running SELECT queries on them
visual.caption: Measured by running the tables in SQLite.

slides.narration: Degree counts columns. Cardinality counts rows. These values were measured by actually running each imagined table in a database, so you can trust them. Notice that the student relation has four columns and five rows, so its degree is four and its cardinality is five. Never count the heading row.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: degree and cardinality after changes
slides.body_md: The shop's ITEM relation gains a column **Shelf**, then two new items are inserted. Find the new degree and cardinality.
bullets: A new **column** changes only the degree: 5 + 1 = 6.
Check by counting the table again after the changes.

visual.alt: Worked example table: ITEM starts with degree 5 and cardinality 6; adding a column makes the degree 6; inserting two items makes the cardinality 8
visual.caption: A column changes the degree; a row changes the cardinality.

slides.narration: Here is a typical exam question. The shop adds one column and then inserts two items. Adding a column changes only the degree, so it goes up by one. Adding rows changes only the cardinality, so it goes up by two. Deleting a row would lower the cardinality, and dropping a column would lower the degree.

slides.heading: Properties of a relation

rows: Each attribute has a unique name
So that every value can be referred to
One phone number per cell, not a list
Order of tuples does not matter
A relation is a set of rows
Order of attributes does not matter

visual.alt: Table of five properties of a relation: unique attribute names, atomic values, no identical tuples, order of tuples does not matter, order of attributes does not matter

slides.narration: A relation follows a few rules. Every attribute has its own name. Each cell holds one single value, so you would not squeeze two phone numbers into one cell. No two tuples are exactly alike. And the order of rows and of columns carries no meaning, because a relation is a set of rows found by their values.

slides.heading: Quick check: count the attributes
slides.body_md: What is the degree of the ITEM relation?
slides.narration: Count the column names in the heading, not the rows.

slides.heading: Cartesian product: every row with every row
slides.body_md: The **Cartesian product** A × B pairs **every** tuple of A with **every** tuple of B.

visual.alt: Table of a Cartesian product: STUDENT has degree 4 and cardinality 5, FEES has 4 and 4; the product has degree 8 and cardinality 20
visual.caption: Degrees add, cardinalities multiply (measured by running SELECT * FROM STUDENT, FEES).

slides.narration: The Cartesian product pairs each row of one relation with each row of the other. So the number of rows multiplies, and every result row carries all the columns of both relations, so the number of columns adds. These figures were checked by running the product of the student and fee relations.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: size of a product
slides.body_md: Find the degree and cardinality of DOCTOR × PATIENT for Seva Hospital, and how many of its rows are meaningful.
bullets: Meaningful rows: only those where DOCTOR.DocID matches PATIENT.DocID.

rows: keep rows where the DocID values match

visual.alt: Worked example table: DOCTOR times PATIENT has degree 8 and cardinality 15; keeping only rows with matching DocID leaves 5
visual.caption: Imagined Seva Hospital data.

slides.narration: Apply the two rules. The degrees add to eight and the cardinalities multiply to fifteen. But most of those fifteen rows pair a patient with a doctor who is not treating them. If we keep only the rows where the doctor identity numbers match, five meaningful rows remain, one for each patient. You will meet this idea again as a join.

slides.heading: Quick check: rows in a product
slides.body_md: STUDENT has 5 tuples and FEES has 4. How many tuples are in STUDENT × FEES?
slides.narration: Each student row pairs with every fee row.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Redundancy, inconsistency, unavailability, unauthorised access, dependence
Software that stores, checks and controls access (MySQL)
Tuple = row, attribute = column, domain = allowed values

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: five file-system problems, what a DBMS is, relation terms, degree and cardinality, and the Cartesian product rule

slides.narration: To sum up: separate files cause redundancy, inconsistency, unavailability, unauthorised access and data dependence. A database management system such as MySQL solves these. Data sits in relations, made of tuples and attributes, with each attribute drawing values from a domain. Degree counts columns, cardinality counts rows, and in a product degrees add while cardinalities multiply.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
slides.body_md: **How marks are given:** 1 mark for a correct count with no working; 2 marks need the definition *and* the value from the given table; 3–5 marks expect each point tied to the scenario.

rows: Counting the heading row in the cardinality
Saying a DBMS removes all repetition
It controls redundancy; foreign keys repeat on purpose

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes in Part 1 with the correct ideas: do not count the heading row, do not swap degree and cardinality, add degrees in a product, a DBMS controls rather than removes redundancy

slides.narration: Common slips: counting the heading row, swapping degree and cardinality, and multiplying degrees in a product. In two-mark answers, write the definition and then the value from the table given. In longer answers about file systems, link every problem to the scenario in the question, such as the school or the shop.

decks.title: Database Concepts — Part 2: Keys
goals: Identify candidate, primary and alternate keys in a relation
Identify foreign keys and explain referential integrity
Choose a suitable key, including a composite key, and justify it

slides.heading: Keys in a relational database
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **candidate**, **primary**, **alternate** and **foreign** keys, **referential integrity** and **composite** keys.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: why keys, candidate keys, primary and alternate keys, foreign keys, referential integrity and composite keys
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: A database must be able to point at exactly one row, and to link rows across tables. Keys make both possible. In this part we test which attributes can be keys, choose a primary key, and see how foreign keys keep linked tables correct.

slides.heading: Why keys?
slides.body_md: To update or delete **one** student, the DBMS must be able to tell every tuple apart.

visual.alt: Table of the imagined STUDENT relation: two students share the name Kabir Das, one in 12A and one in 12B
visual.caption: Imagined records; two students share a name.

slides.narration: Look at this table. Two different students are both called Kabir Das. If the office says change the class of Kabir Das, which row should change? A name cannot tell them apart. We need an attribute whose value is different for every student. That is the idea of a key.

slides.heading: Candidate keys
slides.body_md: A **candidate key** is an attribute (or set of attributes) that is **unique** for every tuple and **never empty**.

visual.alt: Table testing each attribute of the imagined STUDENT relation: AdmNo and LibCard are unique and never empty, so they are candidate keys; Name and Class repeat, so they are not
visual.caption: Checked by counting matching rows in SQLite.

slides.narration: To find candidate keys, test each attribute. Is it unique for every row? Is it never empty? Admission number passes both tests, and so does the library card number. Name fails because Kabir Das appears twice, and Class fails because twelve A appears twice. So this relation has two candidate keys.

slides.heading: Primary and alternate keys
slides.body_md: Choose **one** candidate key as the **primary key**. The others become **alternate keys**.

visual.alt: Flow: the candidate keys AdmNo and LibCard; AdmNo is chosen, so it becomes the primary key and LibCard becomes the alternate key
visual.caption: From candidate keys to primary and alternate keys

slides.narration: From the candidate keys, the designer chooses one to be the primary key, usually the shortest and most stable. Here the admission number is chosen. The library card number is still unique, so it becomes an alternate key. A table has exactly one primary key but may have several alternate keys.

slides.heading: Quick check: the key not chosen
slides.body_md: DOCTOR has candidate keys DocID and RegNo. DocID is the primary key. What is RegNo?
slides.narration: Remember what happens to a candidate key that is not chosen.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: keys of SUPPLIER
slides.body_md: Annapurna Stores (imagined) records suppliers as SUPPLIER(SupCode, SName, City, LicenceNo). Identify the keys.
bullets: Step 1 — Unique and never empty? SupCode and LicenceNo.
Step 3 — Primary key: SupCode (short code made by the shop).
Step 4 — Alternate key: LicenceNo. SName and City may repeat: not keys.

visual.alt: Worked example table for the imagined SUPPLIER relation: SupCode is the primary key, LicenceNo the alternate key, and SName and City are not keys

slides.narration: Work in order. First find the attributes that are unique and never empty: the supplier code and the licence number. Those are the candidate keys. Choose the short code made by the shop as the primary key, so the licence number becomes the alternate key. The supplier name and the city could repeat as the shop grows, so they are not keys.

slides.heading: Foreign keys link tables
slides.body_md: A **foreign key** is an attribute in one relation whose values must match the **primary key of another** relation.

slides.narration: Fee receipts need to say whose fee it is. Instead of copying the name, the fee relation stores the admission number, which points to the student relation. That attribute is a foreign key. The table that holds the primary key is often called the parent, and the table with the foreign key is the child.

slides.heading: Quick check: how many primary keys?
slides.body_md: True or false? A relation can have several candidate keys but only one primary key.
slides.narration: Think about the step where the designer chooses.

slides.heading: Referential integrity
slides.body_md: **Referential integrity**: every foreign key value must match an existing primary key value (or be NULL). The DBMS refuses changes that would break it.

rows: Foreign key must match a parent
Parent still referred to by receipts

visual.alt: Table of four attempted changes to the imagined school tables, each rejected by the DBMS: a duplicate AdmNo, a duplicate LibCard, a receipt for a student who does not exist, and deleting a student who still has receipts
visual.caption: Responses produced by running the changes in SQLite with foreign keys on; MySQL words its messages differently.

slides.narration: These four changes were actually tried on the imagined school tables, and the database refused all four. A repeated admission number breaks the primary key. A repeated library card breaks the alternate key. A receipt for a student who does not exist, and deleting a student who still has receipts, would both break referential integrity.

slides.heading: Composite keys
slides.body_md: Sometimes **no single attribute** is unique. Then a **combination** of attributes forms the key: a **composite key**.

visual.alt: Table of an imagined EXAM_RESULT relation: AdmNo repeats across subjects and Subject repeats across students, but each AdmNo and Subject pair appears once
visual.caption: Key: the pair (AdmNo, Subject), a composite key.

slides.narration: In this imagined exam result relation, a student appears once for each subject, and a subject appears once for each student. Neither column alone is unique. But each pair of student and subject appears only once, so the pair together is the key. A key made of two or more attributes is called a composite key.

sections.heading: 1. Why databases?
sections.body_md:
Keeping records in **separate files** (registers, spreadsheets) causes five problems:

1. **Data redundancy** — the same data is stored in many files.
2. **Data inconsistency** — copies disagree after an update is made in only one place.
3. **Data unavailability** — the data exists but is hard to retrieve in the needed form.
4. **Unauthorised access** — anyone who can open a file sees all of it.
5. **Data dependence** — programs depend on the file layout, so changing the layout breaks them.

A **database** is an organised collection of related data. A **DBMS** (database management system) is software, such as **MySQL**, that creates and manages databases: it stores data once and links it, applies rules (keys, constraints), answers queries, controls who can see or change what, and supports backup and sharing.

sections.body_md:
In the **relational model** data is stored in **relations** (tables). Terms:

- **Tuple** (record): one row.
- **Attribute** (field): one named column.
- **Domain**: the set of values an attribute may take (for example, Age: whole numbers from 0 upwards).
- **Degree**: the number of attributes.
- **Cardinality**: the number of tuples (the heading row is not counted).

**Properties of a relation:** attribute names are unique; each value is atomic (single); no two tuples are identical; the order of tuples and of attributes does not matter.

sections.heading: 3. Degree, cardinality and the Cartesian product
sections.body_md:
**Degree** counts columns and **cardinality** counts rows. Adding or dropping a **column** changes the degree; inserting or deleting a **row** changes the cardinality.

The **Cartesian product** A × B pairs every tuple of A with every tuple of B:

- degree(A × B) = degree(A) + degree(B)
- cardinality(A × B) = cardinality(A) × cardinality(B)

For the imagined STUDENT (4 columns, 5 rows) and FEES (4 columns, 4 rows), the product has degree **8** and cardinality **20** — measured by running the query on the two tables. Most product rows pair unrelated tuples; keeping only rows whose linking values match gives the meaningful ones.

sections.heading: 4. Candidate, primary and alternate keys
sections.body_md:
A **key** lets the DBMS identify exactly one tuple.

- **Candidate key:** an attribute or set of attributes that is **unique** for every tuple and **never NULL**. A relation may have several.
- **Primary key:** the one candidate key **chosen** to identify tuples. Exactly one per relation; unique and NOT NULL.
- **Alternate key:** a candidate key **not chosen** as the primary key.
- **Composite key:** a key made of **two or more** attributes, used when no single attribute is unique, e.g. (AdmNo, Subject) in an exam-result relation.

A good primary key is minimal, simple and stable. Attributes such as names or cities can repeat, so they are not keys even if they look unique in a small sample.

sections.heading: 5. Foreign keys and referential integrity
sections.body_md:
A **foreign key** is an attribute (or set) in one relation whose values must match the **primary key of another relation**. It links the two: AdmNo **in FEES** refers to AdmNo in STUDENT; SupCode **in ITEM** refers to SUPPLIER; DocID **in PATIENT** refers to DOCTOR.

**Referential integrity** means every foreign key value must exist in the referenced relation (or be NULL when there is no link yet). The DBMS therefore refuses:

- a child row whose foreign key matches no parent;
- deleting a parent that child rows still refer to (unless the table is set to cascade).

A foreign key value **can repeat** (one supplier, many items), and its name need not match the referenced key — only its values and domain must.

questions.stem_md: An imagined chain of three pharmacies keeps its stock, supplier and sales data in separate spreadsheets at each shop. Explain the problems this causes and evaluate how a relational DBMS would solve them.
questions.solution_md: Five problems, each paired with how a DBMS removes it, and a brief judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Redundancy:** each shop types the same medicine and supplier details again. A DBMS stores each medicine once in one table and links it by key.
2. **Inconsistency:** a price changed at one shop is not changed at another, so bills differ. In a DBMS the price lives in one place.
3. **Unavailability:** the head office cannot quickly see total stock of a medicine across shops; a DBMS answers this with a single query.
4. **Unauthorised access and security:** any staff member with the file sees supplier rates; a DBMS gives each user only what they need and keeps backups.
5. **Data dependence and integrity:** changing a sheet layout breaks formulas; a DBMS separates data from programs and enforces keys, so a sale cannot refer to a medicine that does not exist. **On balance** the DBMS costs some setup and training, but it removes all five problems.

(a) Find the degree and cardinality of ITEM × SUPPLIER and explain the rule. (b) Explain why most tuples of this product are not meaningful, and how the foreign key SupCode helps pick the meaningful ones.
questions.solution_md: Rules with values, then why the plain product over-pairs and how matching the foreign key fixes it.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Degree** = 5 + 4 = **9**, because each product tuple has all the attributes of both relations. **Cardinality** = 6 × 3 = **18**, because every item is paired with every supplier.
(b) Each item is paired even with suppliers who do **not** supply it (e.g. Rice with Tapti Traders), so most of the 18 tuples are meaningless. Keeping only tuples where **ITEM.SupCode = SUPPLIER.SupCode** leaves one tuple per item (6 tuples), each showing the item with its real supplier; this is how the foreign key links the tables.

questions.stem_md: Compare a file-processing system with a database management system on five points, using an imagined school's student records as the running example.
questions.solution_md: Five points of contrast, each with the school example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Redundancy:** files repeat the student's details in admission, fee and transport files; a DBMS stores them once and links by AdmNo.
2. **Consistency:** changing an address in one file leaves others wrong; in a DBMS one update is seen everywhere.
3. **Getting answers out:** a file needs a new program for each new report; a DBMS answers a new question with a query.
4. **Security:** files are all-or-nothing; a DBMS lets the fee clerk see fees but not health records.
5. **Integrity and independence:** files cannot stop a fee entry for a non-existent student, and layout changes break programs; a DBMS enforces keys and separates data from programs.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** No; it must have matching values and domain, but its name may differ. What matters is that its values come from the referenced primary key (same domain). The name is a design choice; using the same name only makes it easier to read.
